profile.name: Ananya Roy
profile.reason: The slight yellow tint alters color perception on screen, which messes up my design work. While they reduced glare, they were not useful for color-critical tasks.

conversation.question: why do you feel bad about it ..doesn't it make any changes to you
conversation.answer: Look, it did cut down on the glare a bit, I'll give it that. But as a graphic design student, my entire work depends on color accuracy. The yellow tint completely distorts how colors actually look on my screen, which means I can't trust what I'm designing while wearing them. So while it technically made a change, it actually made my work harder, not easier. I can't be guessing hex codes just to relieve a little eye strain.

conversation.question: what are the changes would you like to do in it ..so that it helps you
conversation.answer:
First and foremost, get rid of the yellow tint completely. I need lenses that are 100% color-neutral—clear lenses with a high-quality anti-reflective coating that cuts glare without shifting hues or saturation. 

If filtering blue light inherently requires a tint, then maybe design a flip-up frame so I can quickly check true colors without taking the glasses off every two minutes. But honestly, unless they can guarantee zero color distortion, I just can't use them for my work.

allPersonaInterviews.question: What concerns would stop you from using it?

responses.answer: If the lens coating scratched easily or if the frame material proved fragile over daily 8+ hour coding sessions, I'd stop using them. Also, if they pressed too hard against my over-ear headphones, that would be a dealbreaker.

The yellow tint throwing off screen color accuracy is my main dealbreaker. In graphic design, precise color perception is non-negotiable, so any lens that distorts true RGB or Pantone shades stops me from using them for work.

The constant smudging is annoying. If I'm on back-to-back video calls and the lenses look greasy or reflect glare awkwardly on camera, I’d stop wearing them because maintaining a polished, professional look matters to me.

The cost relative to the actual benefit. Built-in night mode settings on my gaming monitor and phone do the same job for free, so paying a high price for glasses that don't give me any extra relief just isn't worth it.

Physical discomfort is my primary concern. The frames squeeze too tightly behind my ears after a few hours, and if wearing them causes a tension headache, it defeats the whole purpose of reducing fatigue.
I’d stop using them if I realized they weren't actually filtering out harmful blue light wavelengths, or if the frames were flimsy and broke easily when tossed into my bag.
